findings.explanation: ATS is relaxed for a class of connections (web content, media, or local-network addresses), permitting cleartext or weak-TLS loads of that traffic. MASTG-TEST-0322 fails on each of these keys.
findings.remediation: Drop NSAllowsArbitraryLoadsInWebContent, NSAllowsArbitraryLoadsForMedia and NSAllowsLocalNetworking where not needed and load the content over HTTPS. If a specific host needs cleartext, scope it under NSExceptionDomains instead.
findings.title: ATS relaxed for web, media or local-network content (NSAllowsLocalNetworking)
findings.why: Same weakness as the global opt-out, scoped to web content, media or local resources (unqualified and .local names, IP addresses), so less of the app's data is exposed. IP addresses can be anywhere on the internet, so the attack vector stays network.

findings.explanation: The app registers custom URL scheme(s) via CFBundleURLSchemes. findings.explanation: Imports rand() / srand() / random() / drand48(), predictable PRNGs unsuitable for tokens, keys, IVs or nonces. Use SecRandomCopyBytes or arc4random_buf. `arc4random() % n` also introduces modulo bias; prefer arc4random_uniform(n).

findings.why: A non-cryptographic generator is linked. MASTG-TEST-0311 fails only when its output is used for keys, tokens or other security values, which is in FairPlay-encrypted code, so the scan records the API.

findings.explanation: Imports CC_MD5 / CC_SHA1 (CommonCrypto) or CryptoKit's Insecure.MD5 / Insecure.SHA1. Both are collision-broken and unsuitable for signatures, integrity checks or password hashing, but are also widely used for non-security purposes (cache keys, ETags, file checksums), so the finding is a pointer for review.
findings.title: Weak hash primitive (MD5 / SHA-1)
findings.why: MD5 or SHA-1 is linked. MASTG-TEST-0211 fails only when the hash protects sensitive data; checksums and cache keys pass. That use is in FairPlay-encrypted code, so the scan records the API.

findings.explanation: A string matching the Google API Key format ships in GoogleService-Info.plist. It identifies the client; it does not authorise access. GoogleService-Info.plist is a Firebase client configuration. A Firebase API key identifies the project; authorisation is enforced server-side by Security Rules, App Check and IAM. An unrestricted key can still be abused against billable Google APIs, and restriction is server-side state the bundle cannot show. Reported for inventory only; it is not a leaked secret.

findings.explanation: The binary imports dlopen/dlsym, so it can resolve and call code chosen at runtime rather than at link time. That is how optional frameworks, plugin architectures and A/B-tested SDKs are loaded, and it is entirely normal, so this ships as INFO inventory rather than a weakness. It matters only as context: an app that also carries obfuscation (SURV-04) or a data broker (TRK-02) can assemble behaviour a static scan cannot see, and dynamic code loading is the mechanism that makes that possible. Note the limit of the signal: an import proves the symbol is linked, not that it is ever called, and iOS forbids loading code that is not already in the signed bundle. (MASWE-0049)

findings.remediation: Update each SDK to a version that ships its privacy manifest, or add the manifest to the framework bundle.

findings.explanation: NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypes uses types or purposes that are not on Apple's lists: NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypePurposeFraudPrevention, NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypeDeviceInformation, NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypeUsageData. Xcode combines the bundle's privacy manifests into the report developers use to fill in the App Store privacy label, and these values are not ones that report defines.
findings.remediation: Use the NSPrivacyCollectedDataType and NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypePurpose values from Apple's lists that match the data and its use.

findings.why: A collected-data type Apple does not define breaks the manifest's own rules; a policy defect.

findings.explanation: The app ships a PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy declaring 17 tracking domain(s), but 1 further tracker-classified host appear in the bundle and are not covered by any declaration (AppsFlyer). iOS makes requests to the domains listed in NSPrivacyTrackingDomains fail when the user has not granted App Tracking Transparency permission; a tracking domain missing from the list is not blocked, so the user's choice does not reach it. A domain is treated as declared when it matches exactly or is a subdomain of a declared entry. MASTG-TEST-0281 fails on exactly this.
findings.remediation: Add every host that carries tracking traffic to NSPrivacyTrackingDomains, or stop contacting it on a tracking code path. Apple's guidance is that the list must cover the domains the app reaches for tracking purposes, not just the SDKs it recognises.
findings.title: 1 tracker domain reached but not declared in the privacy manifest
findings.why: The manifest declares tracking domains but misses some the app reaches, which fails MASTG-TEST-0281. iOS blocks only the declared domains when ATT permission is withheld, so the missing ones keep working. A declaration gap against Apple's rules and GDPR Art. 13; no standard grades it, so it is info.

findings.explanation: The bundle references 5 endpoint(s) whose owner is based in IL, owners: AppsFlyer. The country is the owning organisation's home jurisdiction from the tracker database, not where a server is hosted, and a referenced endpoint is not observed traffic. If the app sends personal data there, it is a third-country transfer: whether that is lawful depends on the safeguards, purpose and paperwork behind it, none of which is visible in a binary. IL holds an EU adequacy decision, so a transfer there needs no additional Chapter V safeguard. Tracker-class endpoints are among the destinations.

findings.explanation: The bundle references 4 endpoint(s) whose owner is based in US, owners: Apple, Meta, Sentry. The country is the owning organisation's home jurisdiction from the tracker database, not where a server is hosted, and a referenced endpoint is not observed traffic. If the app sends personal data there, it is a third-country transfer: whether that is lawful depends on the safeguards, purpose and paperwork behind it, none of which is visible in a binary. US holds no EU adequacy decision, so a transfer there needs an Art. 46 safeguard or an Art. 49 derogation. Tracker-class endpoints are among the destinations.

findings.explanation: The main Mach-O is encrypted by the App Store. Static string scanning of its TEXT segment won't work without a decrypted dump (e.g., via frida-ios-dump or bagbak on a jailbroken device). Embedded frameworks and dylibs are USUALLY ENCRYPTED TOO (measured 91% across the reference corpus; in half of apps every Mach-O is encrypted), so TEXT-segment string recall is limited bundle-wide, not just for the main binary. What still survives encryption is __LINKEDIT: symbols, imported/defined symbol names, ObjC selectors and linked dylibs, which is why symbol-based detection carries this scan rather than string matching.
findings.remediation: For full TEXT-segment coverage, supply a decrypted .ipa produced by frida-ios-dump or bagbak from a jailbroken device. Resource files, plists, entitlements, symbols, selectors and linked dylibs are still scanned in the meantime.

secrets.publicReason: GoogleService-Info.plist is a Firebase client configuration. A Firebase API key identifies the project; authorisation is enforced server-side by Security Rules, App Check and IAM. An unrestricted key can still be abused against billable Google APIs, and restriction is server-side state the bundle cannot show.
